stories.headline: Crystal Palace's Ismaïla Sarr set to be sidelined for weeks, Pierre Sage confirms
stories.summary: Ismaïla Sarr is likely to remain sidelined with a groin issue until after the international break, Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage has confirmed.
stories.body:
Ismaïla Sarr is likely to remain sidelined with a groin issue until after the international break, Crystal Palace boss Pierre Sage has confirmed.

The Senegal international was last season's Conference League top scorer, but has made just five appearances for Palace across all competitions so far.

Palace have lost one of those five games, while they have been beaten in five of the eight matches he has missed, but the under-pressure Sage will have to do without him for at least the next three outings before the November international window.

When asked about when the 28-year-old might be available again, Sage said: "I think after the international break."

The under-pressure Eagles boss secured a big Carabao Cup win at Fulham on Wednesday night, and will now look to turn Palace's Premier League fortunes around at Tottenham before hosting Hoffenheim in the Europa League, then welcoming Liverpool to Selhurst Park before the pause.

Asked if he might prefer to be taking on their subsequent league opponents -- Coventry and Hull -- Sage said: "Every point smells good, and if we take points against Liverpool or Tottenham or against the other team, it's the same for us at the end, because we need, and we will play all the game to take points.

"We are not in a position to choose one game better than another. We do, we did, and we will do the same with the cups and the league too. That's why we made some rotations, because we wanted to win on Wednesday, but we wanted to create the conditions of freshness for Saturday too.

"At the moment that strategy is good, but we have to confirm that and go until the goal we fixed at the beginning of the week."

Sage confirmed Jean-Philippe Mateta was rested against Fulham but will be ready to start against Tottenham.

Jorgen Strand Larsen continues to recover from the ankle issue he sustained in their 2-2 draw with Besiktas last week, and will train with the group on Thursday afternoon.

Sage confirmed Quinten Timber could also potentially feature in the Spurs clash, which should also feature captain Dean Henderson who recovered well on his first start back from injury on Wednesday.

Palace sit one place and point clear of the relegation zone heading into Sunday's trip to north London, and there has been some suggestion that this weekend could be a major test of the front office's faith that Sage remains the right man for the job.

- Pierre Sage: 'No noise inside' Crystal Palace despite job pressure

- Animal rights group PETA call for Crystal Palace to retire bald eagle mascot

While Fulham was a "good sign," Sage was wary of using it as a litmus test, given the heavy rotation.

He added: "We change 10 players, and the opponent will be different. That's why it's difficult to take a performance, and without the guarantee it will be the same in another context with other players.

"But the idea, the mindset is here, and now we are sure as a group, as a team, that we are able to do that, but we have to do that in the Premier League.

"For the moment, it's not the case. The good sign was we did this thing in the cup, against a Premier League team."

stories.headline: NFL trade deadline grades: Jeffery Simmons, DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson
stories.summary: Did the Bears give up too much to go all-in with Simmons? How did the Colts do in their DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson deals?
stories.body:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline, which is Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

Here are our evaluations for the first deals of trading season, including the massive blockbuster sending Jeffery Simmons to Chicago. Check back through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

Jump to a trade:

Simmons | Buckner | Nelson

Harrison | Jurgens

Porter | McCarthy

Titans trade DT Simmons to Bears
Bears get: DT Jeffery Simmons, 2028 fifth-round pick

Titans get: 2027 first-round pick, 2027 fourth-round pick, 2028 first-round pick

Bears grade: C

Titans grade: A

This trade is extremely fun. The Bears were already an enjoyable and fascinating team with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations. And now they've added one of the game's truly elite defensive players. They also gave up a lot to do so.
The Bears enter Week 8 as ESPN Football Power Index's seventh-best team, with an 80% chance to reach the playoffs and a 13% chance to reach the Super Bowl. When quarterback Caleb Williams has played this season, their offense has produced 0.14 EPA per play, which would be fourth-best in the NFL. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has also been working miracles -- without major turnover luck this time -- but there was a clear need for reinforcements on the defensive depth chart. And now the Bears have landed the best defensive tackle in the league, period.

Simmons has four sacks this season, despite having his pass rush opportunities limited by being on a bad team. He leads all interior linemen in pass rush win rate and ranks fifth in pressure rate. His run stop win rate is above average. And it is hardly a fluke: Simmons ranked second in pass rush win rate (and above average in run stop win rate) while recording 11 sacks last year in a season in which he might have merited Defensive Player of the Year consideration if not for Myles Garrett setting the single-season sacks record.

Simmons is a force and a massive upgrade at an area of weakness. The Bears had been playing 33-year-old Grady Jarrett (who has zero sacks but a solid pass rush win rate) alongside veteran journeymen Kentavius Street, Neville Gallimore and James Lynch. Simmons is an entirely different level of player.

So, Simmons absolutely makes sense for the Bears, and in general, I am strongly in favor of Chicago making deadline additions this season. But there is a compensation limit where a trade ceases to make sense, and I think the Bears ran past it.

Simmons joins a small fraternity of non-quarterbacks to be traded for multiple first-round picks in recent years: edge rushers Micah Parsons and Khalil Mack, offensive tackle Laremy Tunsil, safety Jamal Adams and cornerback Sauce Gardner. The results have been mixed at best for the acquiring team and Simmons, at 29 years old, is the oldest of these players at the time of the deal (Mack was the previous oldest, as the Bears acquired him as a 27-year-old in 2018).

Simmons is under contract through 2030. Assuming that contract is untouched, he will cost $27 million in 2027 and $29.8 million in 2028, with the 2028 base salary becoming fully guaranteed the year prior. That is below what Simmons would make on the open market, but it's still a decent-sized contract for Chicago to take on.

The money saved on Simmons' contract compared to what he would make as a free agent will not reach the expected surplus value of a first-round pick. Even accounting for the high levels of uncertainty in the NFL draft, first-round selections can deliver massive value for NFL teams -- stars on very affordable contracts. The 2027 pick will likely be toward the end of this year's draft, and it seems hard to imagine that 2028 won't be a late first-rounder, too. But I caution against making such strong assumptions -- the Colts didn't think the first-round picks they sent to the Jets last year in exchange for Gardner were going to be as good as they're turning out.

That is the main reason why this is a winning trade for the Titans. Tennessee isn't going anywhere this season, and there is little point in keeping Simmons for a few meaningless wins down the stretch while his trade value diminishes. He's a pillar of the organization, but getting that type of draft capital for a 29-year-old player jumpstarts the next phase of the team. The question wasn't whether Simmons should be traded, but what they could get in exchange. And they got a great return.

Defenders of the Bears will rightly say surplus value alone isn't everything. The objective isn't to have the highest WAR per dollar; it's to win the Super Bowl. And this move increases the Bears' chance to win the Super Bowl in 2026. Maybe in 2027, too. But it likely hurts their odds from 2028 through 2031.

There are quality defensive players out there who could have improved the Bears' defense while costing them less -- edges Josh Sweat or Yaya Diaby, defensive tackle Daron Payne ... maybe even bringing back Mack. I would have preferred one of those moves. They might have gotten two of those players for less than they gave up for Simmons.

The Bears know they are contenders now, which is why they should go for it. But they gave up too much for a (relatively) older player. Given the player, the need and the situation, it's a move I want to like. But I don't think it can be justified in exchange for two first-round picks. -- Walder

Colts trade DT Buckner to 49ers
49ers get: DT DeForest Buckner

Colts get: 2027 fourth-round pick

49ers grade: A-

Colts grade: B-

As soon as the Colts emerged as a team that might engage in a trade-deadline teardown, it wasn't hard to see the dots connecting Buckner back to the 49ers. That became a reality Tuesday.

Though his numbers have dipped, Buckner, 32, can still help the 49ers get after the quarterback. He has four sacks this season, but his pass rush win rate ranked in the 45th percentile among defensive tackles, alongside a 69th percentile pressure rate. That is a drop from last season, when he was in the 90th and 88th percentile in those metrics, respectively. However, that 2025 performance is a positive sign for what he could bring to the 49ers the rest of this season.

Extra pass-rushing help will be welcome in San Francisco, which ranks 19th in pass rush win rate. The 49ers have been without Nick Bosa, who has been out because of a calf injury since Week 3 but is expected to return soon. Their pass defense is the only one of their major units (run and pass on offense and defense) that ranks outside the top seven in EPA per play (13th).

I'll admit I'm a little surprised the 49ers made this move considering they already have Osa Odighizuwa as a pass-rush-first defensive tackle. But he can play next to Buckner -- especially on passing downs. Also, San Francisco's rash of defensive line injuries makes any help welcome.

This type of roster-bolstering move makes sense for San Francisco. The 49ers are the Super Bowl favorites, according to ESPN's Football Power Index. In fact, they are the favorites by a lot, with the FPI giving them a 23% chance to win the Super Bowl (every other team is below 11%). Adding Buckner to reinforce those chances is worthwhile.

The cost was also quite reasonable. The 49ers are surrendering a fourth-round pick and taking over the prorated remainder of Buckner's $13 million salary, assuming his contract is untouched. While compensatory picks are never a guarantee, there's a decent chance that San Francisco might recoup most of that draft capital back via a comp pick if Buckner signs elsewhere in free agency next offseason, especially given that San Francisco is low on 2027 cap space.

That also is why I'm a little critical of the Colts' move here. Don't get me wrong, it absolutely makes sense for Indianapolis to trade him. The Colts are rebuilding, and Buckner is a 32-year-old in the final year of his contract -- of course they should have dealt him before the deadline.

Perhaps this was the best offer Indianapolis received for Buckner today, but they also didn't have to trade Buckner right now. There are two weeks left until the Nov. 10 trade deadline. I would have thought they could have at least squeezed another Day 3 pick in addition to the fourth-rounder. -- Walder

Colts trade G Nelson to Seahawks
Seahawks get: G Quenton Nelson

Colts get: 2027 third-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

Seahawks grade: A-

Colts grade: B+

The reimagination of the Colts is officially underway, with longtime Indianapolis stalwart Nelson heading to the defending Super Bowl champions to bolster the interior of their offensive line.

Nelson, 30, started his career with three consecutive first-team All-Pro selections. His level of play dropped in 2022 and 2023, but the 2018 first-round pick battled back to elite form in 2024, when he posted pass block and run block win rates that were each in the 90th percentile, along with earning second-team All-Pro honors. He earned a second-team All-Pro spot last season, too, along with a 91st percentile and 74th percentile pass block and run block win rates, respectively.

His win rates haven't been quite as strong this season (66th and 37th percentile, respectively), but Nelson's reputation is still superb, and having such consistent results the previous two years suggests he probably remains one of the best guards in the league if we're projecting the rest of the season.

The Seahawks presumably will keep Nelson at left guard and move Grey Zabel to right guard. That will push Anthony Bradford, who recently returned from injured reserve and has played two games this season, to the bench. Bradford recorded 30th and 33rd percentile pass block and run block win rates last season, respectively, so Nelson is a substantial upgrade.

The Seahawks have Super Bowl aspirations but must get better play out of an offense that ranks 26th in EPA per play and 31st in EPA per designed rush. They rank 27th in run block win rate, 28th in yards per designed running back carry (3.6) and 28th in yards before contact on designed run plays. They also rank 21st in pass block win rate. So the team needed some offensive line help and upgrading their right guard or center made sense.

Nelson is on an expiring contract, so unless his deal was altered, the Seahawks will take on the prorated remainder of his $16 million in salary for this season, which is a bargain for the quality of play he brings. The Seahawks could sign Nelson to an extension or a new deal after the season, but they could also let him walk in free agency and possibly collect a compensatory pick to mitigate the draft capital lost in this trade.

It makes a lot of sense for the Seahawks to push their chips in on their current team. History tells us how hard it is to sustain elite defensive success, so the Seahawks need to take advantage while they have it.

This was also an easily logical move for the Colts. The 2026 season is lost, and Nelson is a pending free agent. Whatever value he would bring to the team in the second half of the season pales in comparison to what he brings to the Seahawks, and the draft capital return is more than they would get in compensatory picks (which are never a guarantee, anyway) had Nelson left in free agency. Plus, they save money on the remainder of his 2026 salary.

Ultimately, this is a win-win trade. Considering Seattle's contention window, positional (and overall offensive) need, the draft capital required and Nelson's contract, this is a sound move. -- Walder

Cardinals trade WR Harrison Jr. to Texans
Texans get: WR Marvin Harrison Jr., 2027 seventh-round pick

Cardinals get: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pick

Texans grade: C+

Cardinals: A-

Minutes after the Texans completed their 26-3 blowout win over the Titans, news broke that the rumored trade of Harrison, who was inactive Sunday because of the expected move, would be completed. The Cardinals sent him to Houston for a second-rounder and a sixth-rounder in 2027.

Similar to a lot of trades for young players, there are two simple questions: How much of our opinion of Harrison should be shaped by the league's predraft opinion of him and how much should be based on what we've seen from him in the NFL so far?

Harrison was considered a premier wide receiver prospect and was the first non-quarterback off the board with the fourth pick in the 2024 draft. But his production has fallen well short of those expectations to date, with Harrison amassing 1,578 receiving yards over 33 career games.

That equates to 1.5 yards per route run, which is in the 46th percentile among wide receivers who have run at least 15 routes per team game in that span. That number has been even worse in a small sample this season: just 0.6 yards per route run with a much higher percentage of deep fades and go routes (24%) than the previous two seasons (13%). Harrison's player-tracking metrics have been mediocre but not awful during his first two seasons: 47 and 54 overall in ESPN's receiver scores (with slightly better open scores) in 2024 and 2025, respectively.

Despite a rough start, the 1-4 Texans probably still believe they have a Super Bowl-caliber defense and a chance for a postseason run if they can get more talent around quarterback C.J. Stroud, who has been playing well. I don't think that's far-fetched despite their record. This is not the Texans' first attempt to upgrade at wide receiver. After second-year man Jayden Higgins suffered a torn ACL in August, Houston acquired Kayshon Boutte from the Patriots. But Boutte has managed only 1.1 yards per route run despite Nico Collins missing two games.

The Texans will get Harrison for cheap for the rest of this season and next year, and they will have a fifth-year option on him for 2028. But this move is not worth it if Harrison remains the same player he has been with the Cardinals because second-round picks have real value. Receivers who average 1.5 yards per route run can be found quite easily. The Texans are betting that Harrison can reach the upside he showed at Ohio State, including a breakout season in 2022 when Stroud was his quarterback. Having already played two-plus NFL seasons, the chances of a breakout aren't great, but they exist.

I think this trade makes sense for Arizona. The Cardinals didn't have to trade Harrison yet, but he will be worth more to a contending team than he is to them. It's likely his trade value would sink if they waited until the offseason to deal him. And Michael Wilson already had established himself as Arizona's No. 1 receiver.

Ultimately, I would not have made this trade if I were the Texans because the odds of Harrison breaking out immediately feel too low to justify the compensation. But I at least understand the thought process and desire to maximize a loaded roster's chances of making a real run to make the playoffs and win postseason games. -- Walder

Eagles trade C Jurgens to Ravens
Ravens get: C Cam Jurgens, 2027 seventh-round pick

Eagles get: 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

Ravens grade: D+

Eagles grade: A

First, Tyler Linderbaum walked in free agency. Then the Ravens lost Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic to injury, suddenly leaving them without a center. Last week, Baltimore moved first-round rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane to center but evidently doesn't see that as a long-term option.

So Baltimore turned to the trade market and dealt for Jurgens. It's an interesting and unusual move, because Jurgens is no stopgap. He's only 27 years old and is already on a long-term deal after signing an extension with the Eagles in 2025.

Jurgens moved from center to left guard in Week 2 after the Eagles placed guard Landon Dickerson on injured reserve. It has not gone well. Jurgens ranks in the bottom three in both pass block and run block win rate at guard. But the Ravens are trading for Jurgens to have him play center.

In 2024, Jurgens was a Pro Bowl center who recorded pass block and run block win rates in the 80th and 50th percentiles, respectively. He made the Pro Bowl again in 2025, but his numbers slipped to the 65th and 39th percentile, respectively. He should be a stabilizing force for the Ravens -- perhaps an average to above-average center -- at what has suddenly become a position of need. But the cost is exorbitant.

The Ravens are surrendering a second-round pick (plus a swap of fifth- and seventh-round picks) for the right to pay a non-premium position player market price after this season. Jurgens is due a fully guaranteed $16 million next year. He's due $17 million (non-guaranteed) in 2028 and 2029. Jurgens' $17 million average per year for the duration of his contract makes him the fourth-highest-paid center in the league, behind only Linderbaum, Creed Humphrey and Aaron Brewer, per OverTheCap.com. By comparison, Connor McGovern, who had better numbers than Jurgens last season, makes a little over $13 million per year.

One saving grace for Baltimore is that Jurgens' salary is cheap this season. The Eagles have already paid Jurgens' option bonus, so the Ravens should be on the hook for only the remaining portion of his $1.2 million base salary.

For the Eagles, the loss of Jurgens is the latest blow to an offensive line that is already down Dickerson and recently retired tackle Lane Johnson. Jurgens hadn't played well at guard, but surely they saw him as their long-term center. Drew Kendall, who has played center after Jurgens' shift, has been below average in both pass and run block win rate this season. But the Eagles seemed to believe this was a price too good to pass up.

I understand that the Ravens rightfully believe they are Super Bowl contenders, probably want Ioane to stay and develop at guard and thought they needed to fill their gap at center. Making a trade before the deadline to fix that issue makes sense. But almost certainly there would have been cheaper options out there than this. And the timing is odd, considering that Jurgens is currently in concussion protocol and not expected to play Sunday.

So it seems like the Eagles sensed Baltimore's desperation and squeezed an overpay out of the Ravens. -- Walder

Steelers trade CB Porter to Cowboys
Cowboys get: CB Joey Porter Jr.

Steelers get: 2027 sixth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

Cowboys grade: B

Steelers grade: C+

This is the Cowboys' third trade with the Steelers in the past 18 months (George Pickens and Broderick Jones), and it's their third trade involving a star defensive player after acquiring Quinnen Williams at the trade deadline last season and shipping Micah Parsons to Green Bay last offseason.

It's easy to see what the Cowboys are doing here. DaRon Bland, who first broke onto the scene as a slot corner, was playing on the outside given Dallas' lack of depth. By acquiring Porter, Bland can move back inside, which will allow the Cowboys to relocate 2026 first-round defensive back Caleb Downs, as well. He has been playing the slot, but his natural position is at safety. These are options, not guarantees. Bland might stay outside as the Cowboys instead pursue a strong 1-2 punch at outside corner, with Porter shadowing WR1s.

The salient point is this: Porter can have a rising tide impact on the Cowboys secondary, clarifying the roles of other players and enhancing the whole unit in the process.

Porter is not as tricky of a scheme fit in Dallas as people think, too. His strengths are certainly his length and physicality, such that he can line up in press -- but he has been in press alignments on only 30.6% of his snaps over his career, just above the league average for cornerbacks (24.1%). Porter is a much better man coverage defender than he is in zone, as his passer rating allowed in man coverage over the past four seasons is better than all but Derek Stingley Jr. But the Cowboys are actually running more man coverage (24.8%) under first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker than the league average (23.2%) over the first three weeks.

Of course, early-season rate stats can be noisy. Parker's Vic Fangio-inspired defense will require Porter to play from greater depth than he did in Pittsburgh, and the communication and keys required in that match-heavy system will take some getting used to. But Porter has a valuable and rare skill set in his press-man ability, and premium picks should be spent on players with premium traits. The Cowboys got much, much better in the secondary -- though the move is not without risk.

Acquiring Porter does not solve all their deficiencies; linebacker is still a big problem for this team, and the edge rush isn't far behind. But if the secondary needs less schematic help now that Porter is in play, more coaching tools can be used to hide those other weak spots.

For the Steelers, Porter's recurring back ailments seemed incurable without an extension or a relocation -- what can you do? It's frustrating that GM Omar Khan invested more in third-contract players like Jalen Ramsey and T.J. Watt over a younger, second-contract player like Porter -- Ramsey and Watt will hit their athletic wall far sooner than Porter. Jamel Dean, another third-contract player signed to play corner opposite Porter, now has to cover WR1s alongside Asante Samuel Jr. and 2026 third-round pick Daylen Everette. Corner is no longer a strong position on Pittsburgh's depth chart.

Porter reportedly had contract demands up at the top of the cornerback market, where Devon Witherspoon and Christian Gonzalez recently reset elite deals to clear $33 million annually. I'm not sold that Porter is a top-tier corner deserving of that top money. But because the Steelers let this go on for so long and bleed into the regular season, they were only able to acquire a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick for a young, ascendent cover corner. They could have -- and should have -- gotten at least a first-round pick by playing this differently and dealing Porter in the spring or earlier in the summer. -- Solak

Vikings trade QB McCarthy to Giants
Giants get: QB J.J. McCarthy

Vikings get: 2027 fifth-round pick

Giants grade: C

Vikings grade: B+

A mere 22 days after the Giants signed Jameis Winston to a two-year, $13 million extension, New York decided it needed to trade a fifth-round pick for an alternative at quarterback. Of course, a lot has happened in three weeks.

Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury in Week 2 that is expected to keep him out for at least the regular season. And Winston has delivered two poor performances in Dart's stead, with a 19.0 QBR in relief in Week 2 against the Rams and a 27.9 in Sunday's 12-7 win over the Titans. So in comes McCarthy, the No. 10 pick in the 2024 draft.

McCarthy's pro career has gone poorly so far, which is putting it mildly. He suffered a season-ending knee injury in August 2024, which helped Sam Darnold become Minnesota's starting quarterback. McCarthy was named the starter last season after Darnold departed in free agency but started only 10 games after a series of injuries cost him time. And when he was on the field, the results were not good.

McCarthy posted a 36.1 QBR in 2025 (which ranked 38th out of 45 quarterbacks with at least 100 pass attempts) and recorded a minus-5% pass rate over expected, per NFL Next Gen Stats (43rd out of 45). He threw interceptions at a 4.2% clip (44th), took sacks on 9.4% of dropbacks (40th) and had a 1.8% fumble rate (41st). More alarming is that he did all that while playing for Kevin O'Connell, who has seemingly elevated most of the non-McCarthy quarterbacks he has called plays for.

During training camp, not only did McCarthy lose the Vikings' starting quarterback competition to Kyler Murray, but he then lost the backup competition to Carson Wentz, too. That is a telling red flag.

So why would the Giants trade for him? McCarthy presumably still has some upside based on his draft pedigree, and the Giants are hoping they can profit from him realizing it. But it's hard not to notice the fact that this is John Harbaugh trading for the quarterback his brother, Jim Harbaugh, coached in college at Michigan.

It is difficult to know from the outside which other backup quarterbacks would have been available, but McCarthy still does not seem like an ideal choice. Mac Jones and Spencer Rattler ought to have been the team's first calls (maybe they were). Kirk Cousins probably is off the board with the Raiders sitting at 3-0. Mitchell Trubisky might have been available, considering this already looks like a lost season for Tennessee. And I'm assuming Gardner Minshew II surely must be available, considering he sits in veteran no-man's land between Jacoby Brissett and rookie Carson Beck in Arizona. Stetson Bennett IV could have been an option, too, after the Rams selected Ty Simpson in the first round of this year's draft. I'll grant that some of those options have less upside than McCarthy.

But the Giants' front office should look in the mirror over its bungling of the Winston situation. It's not unreasonable for the Giants to be aggressive in finding a better replacement given how much time is left in the season. But they clearly shouldn't have signed Winston to an extension right before the season if this is how they feel about him!

Even though Murray is a free agent at the end of this season, McCarthy's ship had already sailed in Minnesota after he couldn't beat out Wentz. If he wasn't going to be the Vikings' backup quarterback, his value would likely have continued to drop. To get a fifth-round pick while saving a few million across his remaining 2026 and 2027 compensation (not nothing!) makes sense. They have uncertainty at quarterback in 2027, yes. But that was true whether McCarthy was there or not. -- Walder

stories.headline: WNBA Finals live: Valkyries-Dream Game 6 analysis, updates and highlights
stories.summary: When Golden State and Atlanta play Thursday, a champion will be crowned or the WNBA Finals will be forced to Game 7.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- When the WNBA Finals resume Thursday, will we crown a champion or end up returning to San Francisco for Game 7?

The Atlanta Dream host the Golden State Valkyries in a matinee Thursday (12:30 p.m. ET) at State Farm Arena in a must-win: Golden State leads the best-of-seven series 3-2 and looks to clinch the franchise's first WNBA championship in just its second season.

For the Dream, who have lost back-to-back games after taking a 2-1 lead, it's extend the season or watch the Valkyries celebrate a title on their floor.

If Atlanta wins, the series shifts back to the Valkyries' Chase Center and Ballhalla for a decisive Game 7 on Saturday.

ESPN is on site at State Farm Arena, providing live analysis, reaction and highlights.

Three keys for the Dream in Game 6

Avoid turnovers: Sounds easy, but it has been a struggle, particularly in the past two losses for Atlanta. In Game 4, the Dream had 18 turnovers that led to 16 points for Golden State. In Game 5, 17 Atlanta turnovers led to 21 points for the Valkyries. In short, that means Golden State has scored almost a quarter of its points off Atlanta turnovers in the two games. And in such low-scoring games, the Dream can't afford to allow the Valkyries to get that many points relatively easily.

"It's about playing at our pace, not getting sped up, making the extra pass," Dream forward Angel Reese said Wednesday. "My turnovers both games, I had offensive fouls. So I need to slow down a little and read the game better. I watched a lot of film ... so it's just kind of slowing down and getting to the spots that I know I can maximize."

Hitting open shots: This is another issue that might sound simple, but it hasn't been for the Dream, especially in the three losses.

In Game 1, Atlanta shot 33% from the floor and 16% from 3-point range. Those numbers were 33% and 17% in Game 4 and 29% and 23% in Game 5. Golden State's defense has been the biggest obstacle for Atlanta's offense, but the Valkyries aren't stopping everything. They're getting help from the Dream's shooting struggles.

Guard Allisha Gray has seen her shooting go from 46.3% (33.9% from 3) in the regular season to 34.4% (25.6% from 3) in her eight postseason games. Of course, she has been dealing with an injury to her shooting hand, suffered in Game 1 of the semifinals, which has impacted her scoring ability.

"The biggest thing is to just give myself grace," Gray said of dealing with the frustration of not being 100% during the Finals. "Shots I normally make, I may not make now. But I can't lose confidence in [myself], and I still have to find other ways to impact the game. I know I can play defense. I know I can hit layups."

Getting off to a fast start: Atlanta wants to feed off its crowd energy the way it did in Game 3, a 97-71 win Oct. 21 in which the Dream looked the most themselves offensively. After that game, it seemed the momentum was with Atlanta, but that shifted in Game 4.

Reese said it matters plenty to get the State Farm crowd going early because the best way to crack the Golden State defense is to force the Valkyries to have to play catch-up basketball.

"We're here to get to our identity," she said of a team that averaged 91.3 points during the regular season. "I'm really trying to enjoy it.

"I haven't gotten enough steals. I need to make sure I get more steals, more deflections, more blocks -- that leads to my energy. And when we see a couple of shots going early, our confidence goes through the roof. When you get confidence early at home, that's what helped us get that 26-point win." -- Michael Voepel

Three keys for the Valkyries in Game 6

Continue strong pick-and-roll defense: Golden State has done everything well defensively in its three victories. One thing that has specifically stood out is how well the Valkyries have defended Atlanta in the pick-and-roll.

"A lot of times, it's tough to get the roll because they're doubling down," said Reese, adding that the quality of her screens must be better.

Golden State center Kiah Stokes said the Valkyries take pride in being able to disrupt something that is a staple around the league.

"I think the key to pick-and-roll defense is if you can actually manage it 2-on-2 without requiring too much help," Stokes said. "Because that way, we can kind of stay [with] the shooters. Whereas, I'd say in [Game 5], I felt like maybe their guards were coming off a little too clean and getting open looks. So that was a personal thing for me."

The interesting thing is that even though Stokes didn't think Golden State's defense was as good as it could have been in Game 5, the Valkyries still held the Dream to a season-low 55 points. That should tell you how intense Golden State is on defense.

Win the rebounding battle -- or be close: Through five games, the Dream have outrebounded the Valkyries 189-178. Golden State has won the board battle twice: in Games 1 and 4, both victories. The Valkyries' biggest rebounding deficit was 44-33 in Game 5, but Golden State's overall defense was so good then that the margin didn't come into play.

Golden State coach Natalie Nakase, though, targeted rebounding as an essential part of Game 6. And she sees that being just a general part of better execution from the Valkyries.

"Sometimes it's boring, but I like boring," Nakase said. "I like discipline. It's going to be kind of ugly and gritty, but that's how it's been all season long. We shouldn't be changing in the Finals."

Match the Dream's intensity level: This might be the hardest of all since Atlanta is in a must-win situation and the Valkyries still have two chances to win this championship. But as much as they love playing at Ballhalla -- where Game 7 would be played Saturday night -- they don't want another game there this season.

Admittedly, from the outside it might seem anticlimactic to clinch a title on the road in what will still be the morning hours Pacific time on a Thursday. But the Valkyries aren't worried about any of that. They want to take care of business as soon as possible.

Stokes won three WNBA titles with Las Vegas, so she knows what it takes to close out a championship run.

"We have to understand Atlanta's mindset coming into the game," Stokes said. "For them, it is now or never. It's do-or-die. They're going to give it their all, their best fight. We have to be able to absorb that and still impose our will against them like we've done the last two games." -- Voepel

stories.headline: Christian Yelich honors late Bob Uecker after Brewers' title
stories.summary: Brewers captain Christian Yelich paid tribute to beloved franchise icon Bob Uecker, who died in January, as the team celebrated its first World Series title.
stories.body:
Like so many Milwaukee fans, Christian Yelich took a moment while celebrating the Brewers' first World Series title to remember a man he wished had been around to see it.

"Uecky, I love you, man," Yelich said in reference to beloved Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker, who died in January 2025 at the age of 90. "We did it."

Yelich's tribute after the Brewers' 4-1 Game 5 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays recalled a dramatically different postgame setting two years earlier, when Milwaukee couldn't hang on to a 2-0 ninth-inning lead and fell to the New York Mets in the decisive game of the National League Wild Card Series.

That would be the last game in the broadcasting career of Uecker, who had been calling games through the 2023 and 2024 seasons while battling small cell lung cancer. Uecker had kept that information private up until his death and shared it only with a select group of people, including Yelich.

Uecker capped his game broadcast that night by saying, "That one had some sting on it," then went into a silent locker room and offered condolences to the Brewers players, a moment that was detailed in a documentary on Uecker that came out this year. Yelich struggled to contain his emotions that night as he discussed the hardest part of having a season end that way.

"For me, it was talking to Ueck," Yelich said at the time. "That's kind of a tough one. All the other stuff, it is what it is. It's a tough way for your season to end, but talking to Uecky one on one, it was tough."

Learning from the low moments, that made Wednesday's moment all the more cathartic for Yelich, who has been with the Brewers through all their celebrations and commiserations over the last several years as the franchise had its greatest run of sustained success.

The guy who was named the first captain in franchise history last month accepted congratulations on the field from Hall of Fame shortstop Robin Yount, regarded as the Brewers' greatest player ever. Yount had been an MVP in 1982 when the Brewers made their only previous World Series appearance. He praised Yelich for helping the Brewers finally get it done.

Yelich, 34, and pitcher Brandon Woodruff are the only players who have been with the Brewers since they began their run of eight playoff berths in nine seasons in 2018. They'd been through plenty of heartache as the Brewers struggled to translate their regular-season success into the postseason.

"All those low moments, you don't realize at the time, but those low moments prepare you for this moment," Yelich said. "Without those, this wouldn't be possible. It doesn't feel like it in the moment sometimes when it's happening to you, when you're in those lows. It can be tough at times, but it makes you tougher. There's lessons to be learned from it, and it's all geared towards moments like this. Man, is it worth it."

The Brewers acquired Yelich before the 2018 season, and he went on to become the NL MVP that year as Milwaukee reached Game 7 of the NL Championship Series. He was contending for another MVP award the following year before fracturing his kneecap, the first in a series of injuries he would battle through over the last several years.

Even though Yelich is no longer the Brewers' best player, he remains the face of the franchise in many respects.

"I don't think all of them were clear enough on what it was going to take," manager Pat Murphy said. "Yeli kept speaking it into existence. He kept saying, 'Hey, you know, we're going to win the World Series,' and everybody kind of snapped their head like, 'You believe that? Did you see us play last week?' That type of thing."

Producing in the postseason Yelich wasn't merely leading in the clubhouse. He also was delivering a postseason breakthrough on the field while bouncing back from a regular season in which he posted career lows in on-base percentage (.315) and OPS (.692).

He drove in two runs in Game 2 of the NLCS as the Brewers swept the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers.

In the World Series, Yelich hit a first-inning RBI triple to put Milwaukee ahead for good in a 3-2 Game 1 win, and he went 2-for-3 with a walk and an RBI in the Brewers' 10-1 Game 3 blowout victory. He scored one of the Brewers' four runs in the Game 5 clincher Wednesday.

Now he's finally a World Series champion. He could only wonder what Uecker would have been thinking.

"He's smiling, man," Yelich said. "He's smiling. I really wish he could have been here to see this. That would have meant everything to him. But like we said a bunch, he's been with us a lot. We keep him close to our hearts. This one's still for Bob."

stories.headline: Stanley Cup odds: Sabres' odds hold steady, Ducks' title odds continue to slip
stories.summary: The Buffalo Sabres and Anaheim Ducks have moved in different directions in 2026, and their odds reflect this.
stories.body:
The Buffalo Sabres and Anaheim Ducks had breakout seasons in 2025-26 by ending lengthy playoff droughts. In 2026-27, the former is somewhat maintaining that momentum, while the latter is losing it, according to bookmakers.

The Sabres began the campaign with 30-1 odds to win the Stanley Cup and, one month into the season, they have not budged an inch on that odds board, though they have lengthened slightly to make the playoffs, going from -125 to +105. Anaheim, meanwhile, were 28-1 to win the Stanley Cup on opening night, fell to 45-1 by mid-October, and are 70-1 at the latest update. However, because they play in a relatively weak Pacific Division, their odds to make the playoffs are a not-too-long +120.

The top of the Stanley Cup odds board remained relatively stable week-over-week, with the top six teams' lines remaining stationary. The Washington Capitals lengthened from 11-1 to 16-1 week-over-week, while the New Jersey Devils have maintained the 14-1 odds they assumed after acquiring three-time Vezina Trophy winner Connor Hellebuyck, a transaction that instantly shortened their title odds from 25-1.
