stories.headline: Cavan Sullivan turned 17 last month, but he's already playing like an MLS MVP
stories.summary: Since MLS resumed after the World Cup, Cavan Sullivan has been the league's best player not named Lionel Messi. Does he deserve some MVP recognition?
stories.body:
Philadelphia Union interim manager Ryan Richter remembers it well.

He was mindful of midfielder Cavan Sullivan's mood earlier this season. Sullivan was finding playing time hard to come by for a side that was struggling mightily. Even as Richter was spending most of his time managing the Union's reserve team, he couldn't help but notice the demeanor of a player he first coached as an 8-year-old.

"He was pissed," Richter said of Sullivan in an interview with ESPN. "He wanted a chance to play."

He eventually got it, and he has been taking out that anger on the rest of MLS ever since.

As Sullivan and the Union head into this weekend's game against FC Cincinnati, the 17-year-old is nursing an ankle injury, but his rise has been the story of the MLS season. His 21 goal contributions have already broken the league record for a teenager, eclipsing the 20 recorded by the New England Revolution's Diego Fagundez in 2013. Ditto for goal contributions by a player younger than 17, with Sullivan -- who turned 17 in late September -- breaking the mark of 10 set by Freddy Adu in 2005.

His success has been accompanied by a feistiness, his brilliance often combined with a snarl. Such success has led to chatter that since the resumption of league play following the FIFA World Cup, Sullivan is the league MVP, non-Lionel Messi division.

There is a case to be made for slotting him in just behind the former Argentina captain given the Union's change in fortunes. Prior to the World Cup break, Philadelphia was dead last in MLS, with just seven points from 15 matches. Since the break, the Union have a league-best 39 points thanks to a 12-3-1 record and clinched a playoff spot on Wednesday. That the run has coincided with Sullivan's ascension is by no means a fluke.

When the subject of Sullivan's MVP candidacy is brought up to Richter, one can almost hear the grimace over the phone. Part of Richter's job description these days is to slow the collective roll surrounding his young star, and he's not about to stop now.

"There's time to look back and reflect on stuff like that after the season," Richter said about the MVP talk. "Forget about all the other outside noise of what could be. Let's have a f---ing great session today."

Numbers have also served to cool the MVP talk. According to TruMedia -- which doesn't count secondary assists to the same degree that MLS does -- Sullivan's 15 goal contributions since the World Cup break has him seventh in the league, behind such luminaries as Orlando City SC's Antoine Griezmann (22) and Messi (19). Sullivan's contributions aren't even the most on his own team, with Milan Iloski (18) leading the way. Other players, such as Cincinnati's Evander and Hany Mukhtar of the Supporters' Shield-winning Nashville SC have been utterly consistent over the course of the campaign.

The MVP moniker also gets thrown around rather casually, and with Messi taking up so much of the league's oxygen, it's an easy label to affix to a player like Sullivan who is enjoying a stellar run of form. In some respects, the chatter doesn't do Sullivan any favors. He's still just a teenager -- albeit an extraordinarily talented one -- and the MVP label doesn't tell the whole story of his season.

Sullivan's production seemingly came out of nowhere. His 14 league appearances prior to this season yielded no goal contributions. He had just five in MLS play in 13 league appearances through the end of May, but he logged just 549 minutes. There certainly wasn't any MVP talk during the first half of 2026.

Yet Sullivan's rise wasn't something that just happened. It was the result of some meticulous planning on the part of the Union from the time they signed Sullivan as a 14-year-old, as well as the player's hard work. Every step, from the academy and through the reserve team to the first team, was carefully choreographed. While it's easy to draw a demarcation line pre- and post-World Cup, there were signs of a breakthrough prior to the pause for the tournament, as Sullivan began to get on the field with more consistency. That extended playing time freed up his mind to begin playing closer to his best.

"In the very beginning of the season, if [Sullivan] got 10 minutes here and there, he would try to fit everything into those 10 minutes, and it's hard to play like that," Richter said. "And then towards the end -- I would say the end of the first half of the season -- when he got some extended runs and a couple starts, then he really showed that he could do something at this level."

When Richter took over after manager Bradley Carnell was fired at the end of May, he decided there was no way he was taking Sullivan out of the lineup.

"The first conversation with [Sullivan] was just that he's going to get the chance now, like a real chance, not just put him in and see how he does," Richter said. "It's, 'Cav, I believe that you are a great player at this level and I believe that you can be. Now you get a real opportunity with coaches who believe that fully, and you've got to take it.'"

Sullivan didn't wait for the regular season to try to repay that faith. His mentality has long been one of his best traits, and he was determined to maximize the time that the World Cup break afforded him. He played a match for Union II against the Ivory Coast prior to the World Cup, a period when most of the roster was on vacation. He trained with his brother, Quinn Sullivan, and his father Brendan, a former pro player, to maintain his fitness. He then played in four friendlies against MLS opposition, and impressed every time.

"That was an important period for [Sullivan] because he gained the respect of everybody," Richter said. "And then when the season started, it was no question of 'does he deserve to start?' Of course he deserves to start. He can be a difference maker for us at this level."

Even then, Sullivan's emergence was a bit of a slow burn. He had no goal contributions in his first four matches post-break, but a goal and assist against Necaxa in the Leagues Cup got him going, and there have been no shortage of highlight-reel moments since, for both club and country. These included an audacious back-heel for a goal against San Diego FC that showed jaw-dropping levels of skill and improvisation. Those traits were on display for the United States team against Mexico, when he stole an errant pass from El Tri keeper Raúl Rangel and lobbed him from 35 yards.

Even if Sullivan's campaign has been a few notches below MVP caliber, it has still been a season to savor, and a new face excelling in the league is always compelling. There's also the fact that MLS and the Union won't have Sullivan for much longer; he's slated to join Manchester City in January 2028, shortly after his 18th birthday. With the league calendar changing, all that's left of Sullivan's time in MLS is the 2027 sprint season and the first half of the 2027-28 campaign.

The impulse, then, is to enjoy Sullivan's presence in the league -- and shower him with praise -- for as long as it lasts. And who knows what the next 15 months will bring? This year's MLS Young Player of the Year award seems well within reach, but any future success is predicated on making the most of the present. With the postseason approaching, that is the challenge facing Sullivan and the Union coaching staff.

"This game changes so quick. If you look where the last five months have taken him, where's five months from now?" Richter said about Sullivan. "We have to continue to push every single day, focus on getting better.

"A lot can change in a few months, so let's make that a positive change. Every week that goes by, let's make it a positive. Let's make another step forward. That's my responsibility as his coach, is to continue to help him taking steps forward. I know he has a mentality that he'll continue to push to do that."

If Sullivan does that, then trophies of all sorts should come his way.

stories.headline: Debunk or double down? Judging 10 early-season NBA overreactions
stories.summary: A 29-year-old is the NBA's next breakout star. Miami's Giannis era is already cooked. And so are the Thunder, Knicks and Warriors. Which overreactions are valid?
stories.body:
Welcome to the final days of October, featuring falling leaves, early sunsets, Halloween decorations illuminating the night -- and the yearly pastime of overreacting to the first week of a new NBA season.

After all, small sample size theatre has provided early gems such as:

The sky is falling in Oklahoma City, New York and Miami!

The three-guard experiment in San Antonio needs to go!

Charlotte is already better without LaMelo Ball!

Ty Jerome? Ty Jerome!

With those early storylines and more in mind, let's examine 10 popular overreactions to the young 2026-27 season -- and determine which have staying power. (Note: stats through Tuesday's games.)

The Miami Heat will finish with their worst record since 2008.
Zach Kram: Not an overreaction

For reference, 2007-08 was the last time the Heat finished with fewer than 37 wins, the season that they tanked down the stretch to go 15-67 in a futile attempt to land Derrick Rose in the draft.

Merely by the law of averages, the 2026-27 Heat are bound to improve. They've had the seventh-worst shooting luck on offense, according to GeniusIQ tracking, and the second-worst shooting luck on defense. Miami is actually forcing teams into tough shots, but its opponents have been on fire regardless, making 53% of their midrange shots and 40% of their 3s, per Cleaning the Glass.

On the other hand, the Heat's offense has been stuck in the mud even accounting for that poor shooting luck, and guard Davion Mitchell is the only role player who looks comfortable playing with Giannis Antetokounmpo. There's time for that to change -- but as of Wednesday, ESPN's Basketball Power Index predicts the Heat will finish the season with just 38 wins. That's already down from 46 projected wins in the preseason, and just one ahead of this historical franchise benchmark.

Ben Golliver: Overreaction

Let's be clear: The Antetokounmpo era in South Beach is off to an atrocious start. Instead of building off its blockbuster trade for the two-time MVP with a transformative offseason, the Heat lost Norman Powell to the Chicago Bulls in free agency and settled for adding Klay Thompson, who is a shell of his former self at age 36. On the court, it's already clear that the Heat need another proven ball handler and more shooting, and Antetokounmpo needs more time to jell with Bam Adebayo.

Despite all those challenges, it's reasonable to give Heat coach Erik Spoelstra and his staff a long runway. Antetokounmpo's need to dominate the ball has clashed with the free-flowing offensive system that Miami utilized in 2025-26, and several veteran players seem to be easing into the new season. Spoelstra is a tinkerer who has conjured winning records from less talented rosters, and he'll be willing to trust his younger options if Miami's offensive struggles persist.

It's probably best to withhold judgment until after the Heat's upcoming trip out West. If the Heat can't get right against teams such as the LA Clippers, Sacramento Kings, Golden State Warriors and Utah Jazz, sound the alarm. There is some good news: Antetokounmpo has been productive in Miami's three defeats, averaging 28.5 points, 9.5 rebounds and 5.0 assists after missing most of last season due to injuries.

The Oklahoma City Thunder's title hopes are gone without Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace.
Kram: Not an overreaction

Earlier this week, I went into more depth about the impact of these two long-term injuries on Oklahoma City's title chances. The simplified version: The Thunder's winning formula over the past few seasons has been to combine MVP-level offense from Gilgeous-Alexander with the best defense in the league. The collective loss of Williams, Wallace and Luguentz Dort (via summer trade) bends that second factor out of shape.

Yes, centers Chet Holmgren and Isaiah Hartenstein still form an imposing backline, and Alex Caruso (currently out with an ankle sprain) remains a singular defensive force. But the rest of Oklahoma City's perimeter rotation is now so thin, with enough defensive questions, that I would be surprised if it won another title -- barring a return from one of those injured starters before the playoffs or a significant in-season trade.

Golliver: (emotional) overreaction

Yes, it sure felt as if the sky was falling Monday when Thunder general manager Sam Presti announced that Williams and Wallace are out for the foreseeable future with significant injuries. That's no way to launch a title chase. After those injuries and the offseason trades of Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe, the Thunder are down five of their top six players by minutes logged during the 2024-25 championship season. Oof.

But there's an awful lot of talent remaining around Gilgeous-Alexander, who has been sensational to start this season. Oklahoma City showed its resolve by beating Phoenix on Monday night, and it's worth noting it was only one win from reaching the Finals last year despite an injury-plagued season and postseason for Williams. Presti has picks and tradeable contracts to invest in stop-gap additions before the trade deadline, but he also has a deep roster that was built for the long haul. Count out the Thunder at your own peril.

Ty Jerome will be an All-Star.
Golliver: Overreaction

Only a jerk would root against Jerome, who looks destined for a career year after surviving countless fits and starts to get here. But the Memphis Grizzlies' schedule has been about as soft as it gets to start the season: The Jazz look poised to give up 30 points to any opposing guard, while the Warriors' injury issues and the Kings' general dysfunction disqualify them from being quality wins. Jerome is a talented scorer who more than earned this promotion to lead ball handler, but let's check back in a few weeks. The good news: LeBron James and Kawhi Leonard left the Western Conference over the summer, so there are more available All-Star spots than usual.

Kram: Not an overreaction

Jerome wasn't an All-Star last season, of course, because he played only 15 games. But he has been a star-level offensive player for a while now, even if few people recognized it until he started averaging 30 points. Here are the NBA's leaders in offensive box plus-minus for the 2025-26 campaign:

Nikola Jokic
Shai Gilgeous-Alexander
Ty Jerome
Luka Doncic
Giannis Antetokounmpo
Kawhi Leonard
Victor Wembanyama
Stephen Curry
Jamal Murray
Donovan Mitchell

It doesn't matter when Jimmy Butler III returns -- the Golden State Warriors are cooked.
Golliver: Not an overreaction

The Warriors finally got their first win of the season Monday, but their opening week has been disheartening. With Butler, Kristaps Porzingis and several players missing time with injuries or ailments, the Warriors sat Curry on a back-to-back and rolled out a starting lineup featuring Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Will Richard, Gui Santos and Graham Ike on Saturday against the Phoenix Suns. That five-man group -- great fodder for Charles Barkley on "Who he play for?" -- will combine to earn less than $20 million this season.

Meanwhile, Butler ($56 million) and Porzingis ($19.5 million) are missing in action. There's no way to overcome that math.

Kram: Not an overreaction

We finally agree, Ben. I'm not especially surprised by the Warriors' predicament because this seemed like a gap year from the start, due to all their injury issues and the lack of any real upgrades over the summer. (Aside from Lendeborg, who looks incredible as a rookie.)

Maybe they can stick around the play-in race because the West looks shallower than usual -- the Jazz might also be cooked if Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. are out for a while -- but Golden State's most important goal should be setting itself up for greater success in 2027-28.

The San Antonio Spurs will kill their three-guard starting lineup by Thanksgiving.
Kram: Overreaction

I tend to think debates about starting lineups are overblown because of how much teams mix and match over the course of a game; lo and behold, the guard trio of De'Aaron Fox, Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle has shared the court for just 43 minutes across four games this season.

And while it's way too early to come to significant conclusions using net rating, it's not as if the Spurs have struggled in those minutes. They're plus-15.4 with that three-guard lineup, according to databallr. If San Antonio's coaching staff believes it needs to keep Fox, Harper and Castle in the starting lineup for intangible reasons, then there's no evidence yet that that's a bad idea.

Golliver: Overreaction

Spurs coach Mitch Johnson could be headed for a real saga that might take months to play out. Of course, the critical decision is whether to start Fox, Harper or both point guards. But Johnson could also buy time for that duo to work things out by swapping Devin Vassell for Tobias Harris or Julian Champagnie. Given Fox's enormous salary and Harper's potential, San Antonio must exhaust every possibility before shifting one guard to the bench.

Sacramento Kings coach Doug Christie won't make it to the new year.
Golliver: Not an overreaction

There are so many red flags coming out of Sacramento that it's starting to look like an Olympics opening ceremony. Naturally, the central tension concerns rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr. and veterans Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine. The Kings have turned Acuff loose for 93(!) shots in his first four career games with hopes he will develop into a franchise guard, but his more experienced teammates have good reason to wonder whether that's the best approach to winning.

Christie is stuck, and Ben Simmons' preseason Achilles tear made a tough job even tougher. The Kings look destined to be the NBA's worst team, and that level of ineptitude typically prompts a response from owner Vivek Ranadivé.

Kram: Not an overreaction

The Kings have let go of five coaches since Ranadivé bought the team in 2013. Two firings came at the end of a season (George Karl in 2016 and Dave Joerger in 2019), but the other three came early in a campaign: Luke Walton (2021) in November and Michael Malone (2014) and Mike Brown (2024) in December.

That pattern tells me there's greater than a 50% chance that Christie won't make it to 2027.

The New York Knicks won't get out of the first round.
Kram: Overreaction

I predicted before the season that New York would win fewer regular-season games than a year ago, so I can't profess to be surprised by their sub-.500 start against a tough schedule.

The greatest on-court problem for the Knicks is their 25th-ranked offense, but I expect a prompt turnaround: They rank last in making just 30% of their midrange shots, per Cleaning the Glass, after ranking fifth at 45% with largely the same roster a year ago.

In looking ahead to the postseason, moreover, I would have to see a much larger sample of struggles to consider the likelihood that New York won't be favored in any playoff matchup in the East. The competition will be tougher this year, but the Knicks are proven playoff performers.

Golliver: Not an overreaction

This one is more about vibes than hard analytics. As is often the case for defending champions, the Knicks have had a challenging opening week schedule filled with marquee opponents. In that context, the 1-3 start really isn't the end of the world. New York was in competitive games against aspiring contenders in the 76ers and Celtics last week and then handed the Detroit Pistons their first loss on Tuesday.

But the Knicks' inability to pull out those close games was a reminder of just how charmed their 2026 postseason was from start to finish. Jalen Brunson seemingly hit every big shot he needed to hit, and the one time Brunson didn't come through, OG Anunoby was right there for the one-in-a-million tip-in.

Time after time, the Knicks cheated death with second-half comebacks. That doesn't feel like a sustainable formula now that they've got the target on their backs. Owner James Dolan has also operated like a man who is comfortable with one ring rather than desperate to add another.

Trying to win back-to-back championships has exhausted younger teams than the Knicks in recent years, so no one should be all that surprised if they run out of gas or encounter season-altering injuries before May.

Offseason trades made the Charlotte Hornets' current roster better.
Kram: Not an overreaction (although I'm prepared for Ball to make this statement look silly)

We all thought Charlotte's surprising offseason trades were made with an eye toward the future. After all, the franchise dealt two foundational players and their two highest-salaried players in Ball and Miles Bridges. But the Hornets received so much flexibility and so many valuable draft assets in return that the "one step back, two steps forward" approach made sense.

We might have been giving the Hornets' present-day roster short shrift with that assessment. Charlotte has a winning record despite receiving zero minutes from its starting backcourt, as Coby White and Kon Knueppel deal with injuries. Brandon Miller appears to have taken a leap after signing a five-year rookie extension. And offseason additions Naz Reid and Grayson Allen, who came to Charlotte as part of the Ball and Bridges trades, have combined to average 36.3 points while making 44% of their 3-pointers. Reid, in particular, represents a meaningful upgrade over Bridges at power forward.

Golliver: Overreaction

The jury is still out on the Hornets given the injuries you mentioned and their weak quality of competition to date. With that said, the decision to trade Bridges is already shaping up to be one of those moves they will never regret.

Charlotte's short-term success will be determined by Miller's ability to consistently flex his muscles as an alpha scorer and Knueppel's comfort handling greater playmaking duties. Beyond that, Hornets ownership must demonstrate a willingness to spend to build around that budding duo.

The Ball trade could wind up as a win-win for Charlotte and Minnesota, but at some point, the Hornets will need to prioritize talent acquisition and retention rather than careful cap management. Otherwise, they're spinning their wheels.

Walker Kessler should be on Team USA in 2028.
Golliver: Not an overreaction

Before the season, the Lakers argued that Kessler was worth paying a premium price in draft picks in their summer sign-and-trade with the Jazz because it's incredibly difficult to find centers at his age (25) with the ability to finish plays on offense and credibly protect the paint on defense.

Grant Hill, Spoelstra and USA Basketball would be wise to target big men with that exact skill set for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, especially if Joel Embiid, Anthony Davis and James opt not to return after winning gold in Paris. Adebayo, Holmgren, Jackson and Evan Mobley could all be in the mix, but Kessler brings a level of sheer size and physicality that those players lack. Wouldn't it be helpful to have a traditional center to deploy with Wembanyama and Jokic looming as threats to the U.S. dynasty?

Kram: Overreaction

You cited the Grizzlies' schedule when cautioning about Jerome's hot start. I'll do the same for Kessler, whose two big games to date came against a Warriors team that didn't start a center and a Clippers team with Isaiah Jackson in the middle. That's not exactly Wembanyama- and Jokic-level competition.

Kessler does have international experience, as he was a deep reserve for the unsuccessful 2023 World Cup squad. I believe he's on the long list of American big men for 2028, but I would need much more evidence to place him higher in the pecking order.

The Chicago Bulls will be the worst team in the East.
Golliver: Not an overreaction

For all the preseason talk about improved parity this season thanks to the new lottery rules, there are still some pretty bad teams. The Bulls, Bucks and Nets have all looked like viable contenders to finish with the conference's worst record. (And yet, somehow, the Heat have been harder to watch than all of them.)

The scary part about Chicago's start is how thoroughly Toronto and Boston thumped the Bulls. While the Bulls want to play fast under new coach Tiago Splitter, they're just getting completely run off the court by good teams.

There's obviously no reason to panic if the blowout losses mount: Caleb Wilson should be encouraged to play free and make mistakes, and Chicago's new front office should focus on which of its veteran players look like long-term fits around the promising rookie forward. And is it too early to predict the Bulls will be getting rid of players at the trade deadline?

Kram: Overreaction

The Bulls rank dead last in offensive efficiency, but I believe that's more a product of bad luck than bad process. According to GeniusIQ tracking, the Bulls rank fourth in quantified shot probability, which accounts for factors such as location, defender distance and shooter talent. But the Bulls have underperformed that shot quality by 11.1%, which ranks last by a mile. For context, the largest gap for any team over the full 2025-26 season was just 1.7% -- so Chicago's shotmaking is bound to improve.

That doesn't mean I think the Bulls will reach the play-in tournament or anything so lofty. But I do believe that they'll play more like a typical rebuilding team going forward, rather than losing every other game by blowout margins.

stories.headline: Sergio Pérez's F1 second act: Red Bull regrets, redemption and a fresh start at Cadillac
stories.summary: Sergio Pérez reflects on his Red Bull exit, finding happiness beyond F1 and rediscovering his love of racing as he prepares for his 300th grand prix.
stories.body:
Sergio Pérez had to leave Formula 1 and come back again to realise there's more to life than just racing. Now he's got his retirement home office all sorted for whenever he walks away a second time.

It's a proper office, Pérez assures ESPN, complete with a desk, a busy calendar and plenty of business to attend to. He has investments to oversee, projects to develop and a charitable foundation to run. He's certainly not short of things to keep himself occupied.

There is, for now, the small matter of finishing his Formula 1 career his own way.

On Sunday Pérez, who returned this year with the upstart Cadillac team, will celebrate his 300th grand prix in front of his adoring crowd in Mexico City, a place which returned to the F1 schedule in 2015 largely due to his superstar status at home. It's a remarkable milestone borne out of fluke and one made more remarkable by the fact that not long ago it seemed his career was done for good.

- Nate Saunders on the contradictions of Austin's COTA

- How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico City

- Fernando Alonso slams 'low quality bottom third of the grid'

Worst of all, it looked like Pérez's career had ended with the bitter taste of not being on his own terms. His four years as Max Verstappen's teammate at Red Bull -- the toughest gig on the grid -- had delivered race victories and a runner-up finish in the championship, but a promising start to 2024 gave way to a prolonged slump. By the end of the season, he was out of a drive.

In hindsight, getting through that stint of his career now is a remarkable thing.

"I'm amazed at how I did it," Pérez tells ESPN. "I don't think there are many drivers in Formula 1 who could survive that amount of challenge, I'm extremely proud of how I handled myself, in the car, out of the car, mentally, like everything I went through.

"I'm extremely proud of that period, because it was not just about driving the car, it was a lot of things, and that's really it," he adds, referencing the difficult days of 2024.

Red Bull has undergone a lot of change since he left there. Pérez's old team boss Christian Horner and the company's long-time racing advisor Helmut Marko, who famously squabbled over driver decisions for years, both left the team the following year.

"I always knew that the Red Bull period was a very special one, you know, because of all the circumstances there, I never had the opportunity to really show my proper talent there, just because how the team operates."

Pérez's year on the sidelines in 2025 and return with the upstart Cadillac team this year provided that opportunity. The Mexican driver has impressed at the struggling backmarker outfit with strong qualifying and race pace since the beginning of the season and he now has a contract to be with the team until the end of 2029. While he wanted to remind fans who the real Sergio Pérez was, he admits he had to remind himself too.

"I came back because I enjoyed a lot the racing aspect, but I had a lot of points to prove to myself, you know, like, the way I left Red Bull, I knew that it was not fair to my speed."

The 36-year-old has dismissed the notion of racing into his forties like Fernando Alonso, who will turn 46 racing for Aston Martin next season, but he's clearly not ready to walk away just yet.

Though Pérez's career has not seen him join the likes of Alonso and former teammate Verstappen as world champions, he can boast three pole positions, six wins and, as of Sunday, a triple century of race starts. That will see him move into seventh on the all-time list, overtaking Sebastian Vettel's 299. Even if he can't boast the world titles of an Alonso or Vettel, he now views all of it through a very different lens.

"There are so many drivers around the world that would dream to have the career I've had, so it's like everything in life, you always want more, but I think you have to be happy with what you have," Pérez said. "Obviously, I would have liked to be a world champion, you know, by now, but, it depends on a lot of factors. Unfortunately, Formula 1 is not just dependent on your speed and your talent, it depends on having the right surroundings, having the right support around you and all of that, and unfortunately I never had the chance in my career to be a world champion."

Dad time and a home office

Pérez's year out gave him the chance to live a life removed from the grid.

It gave him the chance to spend time with his children. He is one of just four dads on the Formula 1 grid -- former teammate Verstappen, Alonso and Nico Hülkenberg are the others.

"They have some catching up to do! I have four," he joked. Being a dad and having time to properly spend with them, away from the gruelling schedule of an F1 race season, was one of the things he repeatedly reflected on when unveiled as a Cadillac driver at the start of the season.

Clearly, it has given Pérez a grounding not many other drivers have.

"It's when life gets so much better. You realise what you work for. You have all this responsibility next to you. This is the biggest victory a human can have, to have kids, for me it's the most special. I respect people who don't want to have kids, everyone finds their happiness the way they have to, the most important thing is their happiness, but for me it's the biggest thing in life, having kids."

In his year away from F1, Pérez could finally be properly focused on family life.

When asked by ESPN if it's a proper home office set-up, he laughs.

"Yeah, it's a proper office." It's a funny mental image and a long way removed from life at 300 km/h. An F1 driver, usually squeezed inside the cockpit, visor down, focused on the road ahead, instead sat in a nice quiet office environment, working through emails on a laptop with a coffee on the desk.

"It's a bit like that," he laughs. "When I'm not racing, I'm properly into my things, into my businesses, I enjoy that, I love it. I have my office where I look at things, at my schedule, at the calendars. I do very little related to racing though."

"I like business, I like to run my things, my family office, looking for new opportunities, I get involved a lot. I love my foundation, doing things for charity. I love looking for new projects, meeting the right people, hiring good people, all of that, you know, I have a passion for that."

Pérez is also passionate about his charitable work through the Fundación Checo Pérez, which supports disadvantaged children across Mexico through educational programmes, healthcare initiatives and improvements to children's homes. More than anything else, Pérez wants to give back to the country which will welcome him back as a returning hero this weekend.

"I want to push a lot in Mexico, to bring a lot of capital into my country. I believe there's a massive opportunity there, being involved with some good brands, I would like to carry on with some of the great brands I've worked with, do a lot more for my foundation as well."

The milestone race

You wouldn't know Pérez has never won a world championship if you've ever been around him before a grand prix in Mexico. His status at home is legendary and it was even before he claimed an overdue first race victory for Racing Point at the 2020 Sakhir Grand Prix, the one which earned him the move to Red Bull the following season. At home, he's always been revered.

His podiums at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriquez in 2021 and 2022 were high points, but his 2024 visit -- which could so easily have been his last -- the lowest. He qualified 18th and then languished a lap down at the finish, a result which seemed to perfectly sum up his whole situation at Red Bull at the time. Even if he now returns with a backmarking team, he gets a chance to do it over again.

"Just having that moment back again, with all the fans ... it will be very special. Because at one stage it was like, 'we probably won't see this again ever,' you know? And it didn't end the right way. But all of a sudden we've managed to come back and they've been really supportive of me and the team."

The milestone itself only crystallised late due to world events. Coming into the season, it was due to be his 301st. The cancellation of Bahrain and Saudi Arabia's races at the start of the year due to the Iran war then meant it was due to be his 299th, but Bahrain's deal to hold its race in Malaysia a month before Mexico City's event knocked it into the perfect 300 mark. "It couldn't really be any better, you know?" he said, smiling. "To be able to celebrate my 300th race in front of my family, friends, fans and all the sponsors that have supported me."

Pérez's new deal means he should have more opportunities to race in front of his home crowd in Mexico City. But whenever he does decide to walk away, Perez finally seems to be at peace with what comes next.

stories.headline: AFL 2027 fixture: Five must-watch games in the first month
stories.summary: The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month.
stories.body:
The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month of action.

Get the popcorn ready and get set to enjoy these absolute belters in the new year.

5. Port Adelaide vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 4, Adelaide Oval, Sunday, April 8, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Make no mistake, when Zak Butters returns to Adelaide Oval to face his old mob for the first time since departing, it's going to be incredibly spicy.

In a move that shocked absolutely nobody, Butters left Port Adelaide during the 2026 trade period, inking a long-term deal with the Western Bulldogs. It's a brutal blow for the Power, and his ex-teammates will be sure to give him a hard time when they share the field in Round 4. You just know it's going to be on for young and old!

The AFL also made the move to schedule this blockbuster game as the closer to next year's Gather Round. It means far more bodies will be in Adelaide that weekend and a greater number of eyeballs on the clash.

4. Hawthorn vs. Geelong - Round 2, MCG, Monday, March 29, 3:15pm (AEDT)
The traditional Easter Monday clash between the Hawks and Cats is always on our shortlist of early season must-watch games, and next year will be no exception.

Both of these clubs are in the premiership window. Both clubs have added high-profile players this offseason. Both clubs have fanbases that bring an electric energy to Easter Monday at the MCG.

This one is also set to be a fascinating coaching battle between Chris Scott and Sam Mitchell, two of the game's best tacticians, who will go head-to-head just as much as the players on the field.

3. Fremantle vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 1, Optus Stadium, Thursday, March 18, 8:10pm (AEDT)
This Round 1 game in the west is simply oozing with intrigue.

Of course, the question on everyone's mind is how the Dockers back up after having this year's premiership ripped away from them in harrowing circumstances. Does it galvanise the club? Will we see 'Wharfie Time'? Surely not!

For the Bulldogs, they landed the biggest fish of the off-season in superstar midfielder Zak Butters. This will be the first opportunity to watch him play in his new colours, lining up in the middle alongside skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards.

2. Brisbane vs. Collingwood - Round 2, Gabba, Thursday, March 25, 7:50pm (AEDT)
Reigning premier Brisbane will unfurl its latest flag in Round 2 when it hosts Collingwood in its first home game of the season, a clash that has blockbuster written all over it.

The Lions are looking to become just the second team ever to win four consecutive flags (joining, you guessed it, Collingwood from 1927 to 1930) but will be doing it without superstar midfielder Lachie Neale. The two-time Brownlow medallist departed for the Magpies this offseason, making this early season contest between the two clubs extra intriguing.

Plus, any opportunity to watch current Brownlow medallist Nick Daicos play footy is reason in itself to tune in!

1. Hawthorn vs. Brisbane - Round 1, MCG, Friday, March 19, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Thankfully we don't have to wait long for the Hawks and Lions -- quite possibly the competition's two best teams -- to square off in 2027. And if this game delivers even 70% of what these sides dished up in this year's epic preliminary final, then we're in for an absolute treat!

Many have labelled Brisbane's thrilling win over Hawthorn this past September as the greatest game of footy played this century. That in itself should be enough of a reason for their next clash to simply be must-watch.

There will be extra intrigue with both teams given this clash falls in Round 1. For the Lions, they will be looking to navigate life without both superstar midfielder Lachie Neale and master coach Chris Fagan, while the Hawks will be attempting to integrate recruits Zach Merrett and Ben King into their line-up.

stories.headline: It's still the age of Volkanovski in MMA pound-for-pound rankings
stories.summary: At age 38, UFC featherweight champion makes big jump in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
Alexander Volkanovski made a bold statement at UFC 333 that, even at age 38, he isn't ready to surrender his place among the greatest in MMA. The ESPN pound-for-pound voting panel took note.

On the strength of Volkanovski's second-round knockout of previously undefeated Movsar Evloev on Saturday, the UFC featherweight champion makes a big jump in the latest men's rankings. Volkanovski is No. 2, after entering the weekend five positions lower.

Volkanovski was so impressive that he outshined the co-main event performance of Petr Yan, who defended the men's bantamweight title by beating former champion Merab Dvalishvili. Yan drops one spot to No. 3, the position Dvalishvili used to occupy. Dvalishvili is now tied for eighth after his second straight loss to Yan in their fiery trilogy.

The other significant change near the top of the rankings is the disappearance of Tom Aspinall. The former UFC heavyweight champion is still healing from eye injuries suffered in a no-contest against Ciryl Gane in October 2025. Because Aspinall has not fought in over a year, he is ineligible for the rankings.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Oct. 28. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 29-4

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Movsar Evloev, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

3. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: 2

Record: 21-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 4

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: Jan. 30 vs. Manel Kape

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

T-8. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: 3

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

T-8. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: Dec. 12 vs. Sergei Pavlovich

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.

Other fighters receiving votes: Alexandre Pantoja and Sean Strickland.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Ilia Topuria; 4. Alexander Volkanovski; 5. Joshua Van; 6. Arman Tsarukyan; 7. Merab Dvalishvili; 8. Ciryl Gane; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Justin Gaethje.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Gaethje; 4. Topuria; 5. Yan; 6. Van; 7. Pereira; 8. Dvalishvili; 9. Gane; 10. Tsarukyan.

Andrew Davis: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Gane; 8. Tsarukyan; 9 Pereira; 10. Sean Strickland.

Dre Waters: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Dvalishvili; 8. Gane; 9. Pereira; 10. Tsarukyan.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Makhachev; 2. Yan; 3. Volkanovski; 4. Van; 5. Gaethje; 6. Tsarukyan; 7. Topuria; 8. Dvalishvili; 9. Gane; 10. Alexandre Pantoja.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which Natalia Silva captured by beating Wang Cong at UFC 332. When Shevchenko is healed up, she'll be looking to take back the belt.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: Nov. 7 vs. Virna Jandiroba

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

10. Virna Jandiroba

UFC strawweight

Record: 23-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Tabatha Ricci, April 4

Next: Nov. 7 vs. Tatiana Suarez

Jandiroba fell short in last October's fight with Mackenzie Dern for the vacant title, but she bounced back in April with a victory over Ricci. Up next is a top-10 showdown with Suarez, who also lost a title challenge last year. The winner will be right back in the championship mix.

Other fighter receiving votes: Joselyne Edwards and Jasmine Jasudavicius.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Valentina Shevchenko; 2. Zhang Weili; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Natalia Silva; 5. Cris Cyborg; 6. Alexa Grasso; 7. Manon Fiorot; 8. Dakota Ditcheva; 9. Tatiana Suarez; 10. Virna Jandiroba.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Cyborg; 3. Silva; 4. Zhang; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Jasmine Jasudavicius.

Andrew Davis: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Fiorot; 9. Suarez; 10. Jandiroba.

Dre Waters: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Fiorot; 9. Suarez.; 10. Joselyne Edwards.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Suarez; 9. Ditcheva; 10. Jandiroba.

stories.headline: Lens fans banned from Liverpool match for throwing flares vs. Brugge
stories.summary: Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling Tuesday.
stories.body:
NYON, Switzerland -- Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling on Tuesday.

Lens fans lit dozens of flares and threw some toward rival supporters and the field, forcing the team's Champions League game at Club Brugge last week to be stopped briefly. Lens lost 3-0.

The club already were on probation by UEFA for fans lighting flares and fireworks at a previous Champions League game at Slavia Prague in September.

UEFA said its appeals judges imposed a ban on Lens selling tickets to fans for two Champions League away games.

The sanction will be served when Lens play at Leipzig on Nov. 24 and at Liverpool at Anfield on Jan. 27. A third game ban is deferred for a two-year probationary period.

UEFA said Lens were fined €80,000 ($89,000) for charges of "lighting and throwing of pyrotechnics as well as for acts of damage."

stories.headline: Daly Cherry-Evans won't consider NRL backflip, backs Roosters' Sam Walker move
stories.summary: Without making any promises, Daly Cherry-Evans has ruled out a second season at the Sydney Roosters, while backing the NRL premiers' hardline stance against Sam Walker.
stories.body:
Without making any promises, Daly Cherry-Evans has ruled out a second season at the Sydney Roosters, while backing the NRL premiers' hardline stance against Sam Walker.

Bound for the English Super League, Cherry-Evans insists he has not fielded any phone calls from Roosters coach Trent Robinson or chairman Nick Politis in the wake of the club pulling its multi-million-dollar deal to Walker to remain beyond 2027.

But even if he does, the 37-year-old won't be answering any potential SOS call from the Tricolours.

"No, it's all done. It's all done," Cherry-Evans said on Thursday.

"Look, I'm so proud of my time at the Roosters, but you won't be seeing me back there as a player."

Asked if he promised, the veteran playmaker said "No", but maintained he was content with ending his 16-season NRL career as it started, with a second premiership to go with his 2011 triumph with Manly.

Speaking from experience, having reneged on a lucrative 10-year deal to join Gold Coast to remain at Manly early in his career, Cherry-Evans said he didn't find Walker's situation sad at all.

"Maybe I'm a little too emotionless with these things," he said.

"It's the game, it's the business. I really admire the way that the Roosters have stood their ground on what they believe to be right for the club.

"That's one thing that has really shone through at my time here, is that they will put the club first over any one individual.

"And then from my point of view on Sam, Sam's doing what's best for him and his family and his future, so that's the thing within all of this is - no one's actually done anything wrong.

"Yeah, the emotions get really high and we all want to see people stay and we don't want to see people leave, and I get it, but at the end of the day, no one's doing anything wrong here.

"This is just a contract negotiation."

Cherry-Evans said, as good mates, he'd been in contact this week with Walker, who is in World Cup camp with the Kangaroos in Townsville, and revealed that his grand final-winning halves partner is remaining positive.

"It's hard to rattle Sammy, or maybe he'll never let you know how much he is stressed, or not doing OK," Cherry-Evans said.

"But from what I understand in my conversations with him, he's going well. He's got good family and friends around him.

"I would back Sam to have a really long career in the NRL. We all wanted to see it happen at the Roosters and I'm sure there's a chance it could happen and still happen, but it's a game, it's a business.

"I know we'd love to see our players play for one club, but the likelihood and the reality of that, it just doesn't happen often anymore."

If the Roosters do release Walker from the remaining year of his contract as the Queensland and new Australia representative becomes a free agent on Sunday, youngster Toby Rodwell is being earmarked as the likely No.7 replacement.

"I love Toby Rodwell, and I think he's got a great future ahead," Cherry-Evans said.

"But I'm not playing hypotheticals with you."

stories.headline: Man City, Bayern among the good, bad and lucky in Europe's top leagues
stories.summary: We're a quarter of the way through the 2026-27 European season -- long enough to separate fact from fiction when it comes to from. Who's been lucky? Who's been good? Who's been both, or neither?
stories.body:
About a quarter of the way through the club season, your place in the table only means so much. In the Premier League and Bundesliga, 14 teams -- including Ipswich Town, Paderborn and even Tottenham Hotspur -- are within six points of the top four. In Ligue 1, it's 13. In LaLiga, 14 teams are within six points of the relegation zone. You can find some separation here and there, but we're just getting started, and we only have a partial picture of how things will end up.

We also know that the table is lying a little bit. We see funky results all the time, and they have an outsized impact when we're seen only a small portion of matches. Still, by this point in the 2026-27 campaign, each Big Five team has played hundreds and hundreds of possessions, and we know who is creating (or allowing) the best chances. Thanks to xG, we also know what that means.

Essentially, xG is a chance creation metric. It obviously doesn't guarantee success, especially in the short term, but over the long haul a team's ability to create superior shot quality and/or volume is more predictive than simply who's putting the ball in the net in a small sample. And by comparing who's generated the most points to who's created chance creation advantages, with a fun trend line in between, we can get a grasp of who is ahead of or behind where they should be.

Who's both lucky and good? Who's good, but unlucky? Who's the opposite?

Here are some xG standouts, for better or worse, in Europe's Big Five leagues.

- Jones: Vozinha's Ballon d'Or appearance was made for us

- Ogden: Man United are a mess. Where are the Glazers?

- Olley: Ballon d'Or is Kane's crowning moment

Lucky and good

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game, but more points than expected

Lazio. Lazio have finished seventh or worse in Serie A for three straight years, and due to an ongoing fan protest of club president Claudio Lotito, they're averaging a league-worst home attendance of 9,515. They've also only dropped two points in nine league matches, and they're tied with Inter atop the table. Pretty wild stuff.

It's also probably unsustainable stuff.

While they've enjoyed a few genuinely dominant performances (like a 6-2 win at Sassuolo), they've also scored 22 goals from shots worth just 15.5 xG. Forward Tijjani Noslin, winger Gustav Isaksen and midfielder Kenneth Taylor have combined for nine goals from 3.9 xG; I probably don't have to spell out how unsustainable that is. Lazio have stockpiled enough points to remain in the Champions League hunt for a while, but there's a goal-scoring slump in their future, whether or not there are fans in the stands to see it.

Atletico Madrid. Diego Simeone scoffs at your advanced stats. Over the past 12 full seasons, Atletico have produced a goal differential higher -- and in some cases, much higher -- than their xG differential 11 times. In fact, over the Simeone era, their GD in league play (+504) is 46% higher than their xGD (+346.0). Dark magic is a real thing, I guess.

Atleti have always been happy allowing opponents to hammer shots into a box cluttered by defenders (with the immaculate Jan Oblak behind them), and they've always had impressive finishers -- Antoine Griezmann (143 goals from 113.6 xG) and Angel Correa (68 from 57.4) in particular -- ready to turn a half-chance into a goal. But even without either Griezmann or Correa, they're overachieving again this fall. Oblak remains excellent, Álex Baena has picked up the "major finishing overachiever" mantle, and in four matches with a negative xG differential, Atleti have scored two wins, a draw and only one loss.

Manchester City. No one else has been Lazio-level lucky this season, but City damn near packed a season's worth of xG fortune into one match -- a 5-3 win over Sunderland in which they generated 2.8 xG and allowed 3.6. It was their only match with a negative xG differential this season, but between that and a 1-0 win over Manchester United (xGD: +0.1), they could have easily dropped more points than they actually have this season.

They have an xG cheat code in habitually excellent finisher Erling Haaland (nine goals from shots worth 6.1), but they've been lucky that their defense (seventh in xG allowed) hasn't been more costly.

Borussia Dortmund. It's been difficult to get a read on BVB this season. They've generated a positive xG differential in all seven Bundesliga matches, and their only losses have come against Bayern in the Franz Beckenbauer Super Cup and at Bodø/Glimt in their North Pole fortress in the Champions League. But after winning six straight before the international break, they sandwiched a pair of frustrating draws around the Bodø/Glimt loss upon their return.

Dortmund are on the lucky-and-good list because their defense has been a bit too successful. They've allowed goals in just two Bundesliga matches, and their four goals allowed have come from shots worth 7.3 xG. Yes, they have a high-level goalkeeper in Gregor Kobel, but opponents have simply missed the target quite a bit, too. That likely won't continue, nor will their current tie with Bayern in the league table.

Como. Como are easily Serie A's happiest Champions League story thus far, having won two of their first three matches in their debut in the competition. In theory, they've balanced those duties with solid league play, too -- they're fourth in the league and only five points from first. But they've been at least a little bit fortunate: They've suffered a negative xG differential in four of nine Serie A matches, but they've won two of those four and drawn in one.

- Who are Como? The vacation-destination club that just rocked Man United

That said, the trends are strong: Since returning from the international break, they've suffered a negative xGD only once and have taken 10 points from four league matches. Including their Champions League stomping of Manchester United, they've generated an xGD of at least plus-1.1 in three straight. They were lucky and good, but they might just be good now.

Good, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Nottingham Forest. If you didn't look at the table, you'd think Oliver Glasner is doing great work in his first season as manager in Nottingham. Forest beat Aston Villa and drew with Liverpool at Anfield, and for the season they're sixth in xG created (13.4), second in xG allowed (9.0) and fifth in overall xG differential. The fundamentals are in great shape.

Somehow they're also 18th in the table, behind even Glasner's direction-less former employer, Crystal Palace. They've turned shots worth 13.4 xG into only six goals; attackers Morgan Gibbs-White, Liam Delap and Chris Wood have attempted 38 shots worth 5.3 xG, but they've put only eight shots on target and scored twice. Forest have generated a positive xG differential in six of eight matches and have somehow won just one of them. That they will almost certainly right the ship in this regard and start winning matches soon, but how many unnecessary points will they have dropped by then?

Brest. After surging to third in Ligue 1 in 2023-24 and qualifying for the Champions League, Brest slipped to ninth and then 12th in the last two seasons. Now they're 13th. It appears the balloon is losing helium.

If the results start matching the chance creation, however, a turnaround is possible. They're second in Ligue 1 in xG differential, well behind PSG but well ahead of everyone else. They've created a dominant xG differential of +1.9 or better in four matches but have somehow won only one of them. Both their finishing and defense have let them down at times, but midfielder Joris Chotard is fifth in the league in chances created, and the combo of young wingers Kamory Doumbia and Pathé Mboup with veteran big man Ludovic Ajorque has created a number of dangerous opportunities.

This is one of France's better teams, no matter what the table says.

Villarreal. Villarreal are third in xG differential and 10th in LaLiga. They have dropped unlikely points to Atletico Madrid (2-2 draw, +2.8 xG differential), Elche (0-0 draw, +2.1 xGD) and Alaves (1-0 loss, +1.0). Forwards Georges Mikautadze and Ayoze Pérez have scored just four goals from shots worth 8.4 xG; in the Champions League, meanwhile, they've scored two goals from 1.2.

Aside from finishing, there's nothing inherently wrong with this squad. They're third in shots per possession margin and fourth in xG per shot margin. They play a pretty possession game -- Renato Veiga is one of only two players in LaLiga (along with Barcelona's Gerard Martín) to already have over 100 progressive passes and 100 progressive carries -- without giving up much on the counter. But they're eight points behind fourth-place Real Betis; they have some ground to make up.

Bournemouth. Only Manchester City, Arsenal and Brentford have led more Premier League matches this season than Bournemouth, but somehow the Cherries have turned leads in six matches -- and positive xG differentials in six matches -- into just two wins. Marcus Tavernier has scored a lovely five goals from shots worth 3.6 xG, but the rest of the team has just six goals from shots worth 10.9. They aren't generating the sizable advantages they should, and they've been outscored 4-0 from the 80th minute on. They're third in xG differential but 13th in the table because of the late leaks.

It could be worse -- most of their unfortunate results have been draws and not losses. But with so many bigger clubs struggling out of the gate, Bournemouth had a chance to establish a good spot in the race for a top-five finish. They're off of that pace.

Bayern Munich. Maybe one day this hard-luck club will catch a break. Alas, the 35-time German champions have dropped points twice -- 0-0 at Schalke (xG differential: +1.7), 2-2 at Augsburg (+2.5) -- despite dominating the early stages of the season as much as ever.

Seriously, though, this is ridiculous:

Every so often, the Bundesliga figures out how to balance great crowds, fun stories and sustained challenges for Bayern, but it doesn't appear this will be one of those years, even if those two draws mean Bayern and Borussia Dortmund are tied in points at the moment. Bayern's xGD is actually higher now than it was after they won their first seven matches last season.

Ballon d'Or winner (!) Harry Kane has gone through his version of a finishing funk (he has four league goals from shots worth 5.2 xG), and Serge Gnabry is in a similar boat (one goal from 2.2 xG). Something tells me they'll be all right.

Bad, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Venezia. It's a yo-yo period in Venice. Venezia were promoted from Serie B in 2021, but went straight back down. They came back up in 2024, went back down in 2025, then came right back up in 2026. And through eight matchdays, they have three points and are last in the Serie A table.

However, they haven't been that bad. This team obviously isn't loaded with proven finishers, but scoring just six goals from shots worth 14.5 xG is severely unfortunate. Forwards John Yeboah, Albion Rrahmani and Lion Lauberbach somehow have one goal from 5.1 xG; they aren't generating ridiculously high-quality shots, but that is still some unsustainably poor finishing. Venezia have generated a positive xG differential in four of nine matches, and they're 14th overall in xGD. They'll have a chance to stay up if their finishing begins to reflect their actual chance creation.

Borussia Mönchengladbach. The five-time German champions finally notched a win last weekend, shocking Stuttgart 3-2. It was both deserving and a long time coming. They had lost their first six league matches, alternating between awful (losing to RB Leipzig and Freiburg by a combined 8-0) and unlucky (4-3 losses to Elversberg and Mainz despite a combined xGD of +0.5).

The club hired former St. Pauli manager Alexander Blessin on Sept. 22, and while he made an immediate impact on their defense, they finally generated some offense in Stuttgart too. American right midfielder Joe Scally and 17-year old left midfielder Wael Mohya each had a goal and an assist in that match, and if Gladbach can generate production like that from the wings, maybe it will offset the black hole of production they've gotten from their center forwards in the absence of injured veteran Tim Kleindienst.

Valencia. After pulling nine points from their first 11 league matches last year and 10 from their first 15 in 2024-25, Valencia have just six points after 10 matches this season. Only Villarreal and Osasuna have been worse at finishing the season: Valencia have turned shots worth 10.8 xG into only seven goals. In matches against Real Betis (1-0 loss), Celta Vigo (0-0 draw) and Athletic Club (0-0 draw) they attempted 40 shots worth 3.3 xG, and none went in the net. Those matches could have easily produced six to nine points ... but yielded just two instead.

Despite average defensive numbers, there's no way to say this team is anything better than below average. But while they're growing awfully familiar to relegation scraps at the moment -- and if you play with fire enough, you will get burned -- I can't say they're actually relegation-worthy just yet.

Troyes. Back in Ligue 1 after a three-year absence, Troyes attempt more shots than their opponents and press frequently. They don't attempt many good shots, but they rank 15th in xG created and 10th in xG allowed. That they only have five points from eight matches is therefore a smidgen unlucky. They've scored only five goals from shots worth 9.7 xG, and they've allowed 16 goals from shots worth 13.2. A lot of that damage comes from one match -- a 6-2 loss to Strasbourg in which both teams generated 2.9 xG -- but forwards Renaud Ripart and Jeremy Le Douaron have combined for two goals on 4.7 xG. Finish at more normal levels, and they'll have a solid shot at survival.

Sunderland. Sunderland were the "stats don't matter" team of 2025-26, ranking 18th in the Premier League in xG differential, but somehow finishing seventh and grabbing a spot in the Europa League. You usually don't have to wait long for what we'll call statistical comeuppance. This year they've actually improved to 15th in xG differential, and they've generated a positive xGD in four of eight matches, but they've won just one because aside from Brian Brobbey (three goals from shots worth 3.2 xG), no one can turn shots into goals.

Sunderland rank third in the league in xG per shot, but they're 18th in goals and haven't scored in a league match since Sept. 20. That puts them at the bottom of the table. A lot of teams are struggling at the moment, so they're not in too big a hole, but after this weekend's trip to Coventry City, their schedule gets awfully tricky.

Lucky and bad

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game but more points than expected

Frosinone. Frosinone have been promoted to Serie A four times since 2015; they have yet to avoid going straight back down. That they're currently sixth in points per game, ahead of mighty Juventus, is a thrilling story. But it's really hard to believe this story will last. They're also 18th in xG differential, having scored 17 goals from shots worth 13.1 xG while allowing 13 goals from shots worth 19.5.

This is unsustainable in obvious ways, but as Sunderland learned last year, if you stockpile points early, you can ride it out when regression to the mean invariably hits. They're already nine points above the drop zone with a game in hand; from here, it won't take too much additional good fortune for them to survive a year in Serie A for the first time.

Elversberg. The most delightful early Bundesliga story is also a fortunate one. Tiny Elversberg, from a town of 13,000 people, have three wins and 10 points from seven matches in their top-division debut. They're a healthy eighth in the table, but they also have yet to actually generate a positive xG differential in a match, and in three one-goal wins they scored 11 goals from shots worth 7.4 xG.

This is an optimistic team with fun attacking ideas, and maybe they can continue to avoid the relegation hunt with bursts of excellence from players such as 22-year-old David Mokwa (1.2 xG, two goals) and 21-year-old Maurice Krattenmacher (2.4 xG, three goals). But they lost 4-0 to RB Leipzig last weekend, and it feels like there might be a few more heavy defeats in their future. Hopefully I'm wrong.

Marseille. Not only are Marseille a terribly disappointing eighth in Ligue 1 at the moment, but they're lucky to even be that high. Their 18 goals scored (first in the league) have come from just 13.6 xG (seventh), while their 18.5 xG allowed (last) has turned into only 13 goals (11th). Last week's 4-3 win over Le Havre featured a minus-1.6 xG differential.

Only Strasbourg have a lower league xG differential than l'OM right now. Marseille do have historically solid finishers like Amine Gouiri and Igor Paixão pacing the attack, and a lot of their defensive overachievement came from a single match -- a 2-1 loss to PSG in which they allowed shots worth 5.1 xG. Still, the fundamentals do not suggest that manager Bruno Genesio is fielding a team worth a spot in a European competition at the moment.

Cagliari. Like Frosinone, Cagliari has stocked up on some early points (13 in nine Serie A matches) thanks to some early good fortune. They've suffered a negative xG differential in six of nine matches, but have won two of those with a draw. They've gotten spectacular goalkeeping from Elia Caprile thus far, but allowing just 13 goals from shots worth 17.3 xG is pretty fortunate.

Strangely, though, it's offset some poor finishing from Cagliari, too: While left winger Daniel Maldini is on a hot streak (five goals from shots worth 3.4 xG), the rest of the team has just three goals from 8.1 xG, and if their own finishing progresses more than opponents', they could remain mid-table for quite a while longer.

Newcastle United. Let's isolate that PPG vs. xGD chart above with just Premier League teams.

Maybe no attack in Europe has defied xG more than Newcastle's, and in two different directions.

- Yoane Wissa: 1 goal from shots worth 3.0 xG (minus-2.0 difference)

- Everyone else: 11 goals from shots worth 6.2 xG (plus-4.8 difference)

Wissa has done a great job of generating nearly one-third of Newcastle's xG by himself, but he's been in a major finishing slump. And it's been more than offset by the fact that other guys can't seem to miss.

Newcastle ranks 16th in shots per possession margin and 19th in xG per shot margin; they've generated a positive xG differential in only one match, but incredibly, they lost that match and have only lost two of seven with a negative xGD. It either works (two of three wins were by two goals) or really, really doesn't (two of three losses were by three goals). And I honestly don't have much of an idea of what to expect from them moving forward. I'm not incredibly optimistic, though.
